about: The first of the two prayers at the ablutions, said while the minister pours wine into the chalice. It asks that what has passed the lips be taken up with a pure heart, and that a gift given in time become an everlasting remedy.

s02.translation: Lord, may we receive with a pure heart what our mouths have received, and may the gift given in time become for us an everlasting remedy.

s03.narrative: Meanwhile the priest holds out the chalice to the server, who pours a little wine into it, and with this the priest purifies himself.

w001.function: The relative with nothing to refer back to: “that which”. Latin can leave the antecedent unsaid where English needs a word for it.

w002.function: Ablative of means: “with the mouth”. “Os” means the mouth here, not the word for bone, which has the same spelling.

w003.function: Perfect. Reception by mouth has taken place, while reception with a pure mind is still being asked for.

w006.function: An ablative phrase of manner: “with a pure mind”. The translation renders this interior disposition as “purity of heart”.

w007.function: Present subjunctive. The prayer asks that what has been received by mouth also be received with a pure mind.

w011.function: Agrees with “múnere” (w010) and contrasts with “sempitérnum” (w015): “temporal” and “everlasting”.

w014.function: With “sempitérnum” (w015), it is the subject of “fiat” (w012): “may there be an everlasting remedy”.
